t: The line we are going to build
html:
The machine is the LogixPro bottle line, the exercise generations of technicians learned shift registers on, rebuilt as a plant. A main conveyor on a raised deck indexes bottles one 40 px pitch at a time past three head sensors, a fill station fed from a soda reservoir, a capper with a rotary cap magazine, a labeler, an inspection camera, a scrap gate and a divert gate. Broken bottles, and bottles the camera fails, are dropped off the deck into a shredder whose chute fills boxes on a box conveyor below, and a second labeler bands each of those boxes with hazard tape. Small bottles go down a catch incline onto a divert conveyor, which runs on under a case packer at the end of the line; large bottles run on along the deck to the same packer. The packer picks large bottles off the deck and small ones off the floor conveyor, 1.7 m below, and packs them four to a case, one size per case, on a case lane driven by a variable frequency drive. Beside the line a mix kitchen makes the soda: water and cola syrup batched in a mix tank, carbonated, and pumped to the reservoir. An operator console has Start, Stop, a Run lamp, a red fault lamp and a blue Reset, a carbonation key, a thumbwheel preset with Enter, and six displays: SMALL, LARGE, SCRAP, BOXES, IN BOX and CASES.

The program is fifteen routines called from the main routine, one per step, and each step is a lesson that leaves you with something that runs:

  1. Run circuit (S1_Run): Start / Stop seal-in, the run lamp.
  2. Dwell and feed (S2_Dwell): a one-second timer while the belt stands, and one bottle per stop from the feeder.
  3. Index (S3_Index): step exactly one pitch on the encoder when nothing holds the belt.
  4. Shift registers (S4_Registers): three registers take the three head sensors once per stop; a fourth takes the camera’s verdict.
  5. Fill (S5_Fill): a bottle under the nozzle gets its large or small charge.
  6. Supply (S6_Supply): the reservoir’s inlet on its floats, the head-tank protection, the tank stack light.
  7. Cap (S7_Cap): a cap from the chute, the cap feeder, the column lights.
  8. Sort (S8_Sort): the scrap and divert gates, the divert conveyor, the box conveyor and the shredder.
  9. Count and preset (S9_Count): the displays, the thumbwheel batch stop, Enter.
  10. Label (S10_Label): an FLS-style dispenser one stop past the capper: the Start / Ready / Error handshake, a latched fault, lamps.
  11. Alarms (S11_Alarms): the program watching the machine: overloads, an end-of-line check of the tracking, a dirty eye, the labeler, the inlet, the packer; a fault lamp and Reset.
  12. Pack (S12_Pack): the case packer and the VFD on its case lane: fast, a creep onto the mark, a speed reference scaled to 0–10 V with SCP, four bottles a case.
  13. Mix (S13_Mix): the mix kitchen: water and cola syrup batched into soda at the 5 : 1 throw, heated and mixed to the recipe, carbonated, and pumped to the reservoir whenever step 6 calls for it.
  14. Hazard tape (S14_Hazard): a second dispenser bands every scrap box.
  15. Inspect (S15_Inspect): a camera checks every bottle for its cap, its label and its fill, and the scrap gate takes the ones it fails.

The steps are numbered in the order they were added to the line, and that is also the order in MainRoutine, with one exception that chapter 9 explains: step 3’s JSR is always the last, so every station’s request is seen before the belt is allowed to step. The lessons take steps 14 and 15 with the labeler (chapter 27), because they use its handshake, and step 13 last, because it changes where the soda comes from.

Guided mode

You can do Part IV with the book open beside the app, or let the app walk you through it. File → New Project… → Build the bottle line (or Guided → Start: Build the Bottle Line Here on an empty floor) opens a panel that follows these chapters one lesson at a time. Each lesson lists what it checks: parts placed at the book’s positions, alias tags made, the routine and its JSR in place, the routine verifying; and, for the steps that do something, what it watches for while you run the line: Line_Run coming on when you press Start, a bottle filled and capped, a label going on. A check turns green when the page sees it happen.

The panel checks your rungs itself. A reference rung is logic verified (one tick) when a rung of yours does the same thing: the page runs both through every combination of the bits they read and write, so the order of the contacts, how you draw a branch, or writing a tag as its alias address make no difference, and a timer or a move must be there with the same operands. A rung that is close but wrong stays open with one line on what differs, and the first one still to write is marked NEXT. In Run mode a verified rung is proven (two ticks) the first time it goes true.

Hints first. A reference rung you can read is a rung you will copy, so each one opens as its comment alone: the job, in words, which is how a rung arrives in real life. If you cannot write it from that, Hint lists what the rung uses, in no order; Shape shows its skeleton with every tag blanked, XIC(?)XIC(?)XIO(?)ONS(?)OTL(?); and only Show rung gives the text. Guided → Hints First turns this off for a project, and Predict First asks a Predict-it question before a rung is shown. Place them for me and Make them for me do a lesson’s layout or tags in one click when you would rather get to the programming. Progress saves with the project; the panel docks into the output window as a Guided tab, or folds into the Guided menu, which shows where you are.

Chapter 16 lays the machine out, chapter 17 makes the tags, chapters 18 to 30 write the fifteen routines, and chapter 31 commissions the line. Every coordinate and setting below is the one the finished template uses, so your machine and the answer key are the same machine.
